segments.text: Maze, level two. We log in as maze two - level one's planted-constructor trick paid off - and the goal is the maze3 password. The gate: /maze/maze2, a setuid maze3 binary.

Recon: file says a thirty-two-bit setuid ELF with debug info. readelf shows the GNU stack segment is read-write-execute, so code on the stack is legal, and this lab runs with address randomization off. The objdump of main is the whole level in a handful of instructions: with exactly one argument, it lea's a twelve-byte buffer, stores the buffer's own address into a pointer, strncpy's the first eight bytes of argv one into that buffer, then calls the pointer. So the eight copied bytes ARE the code, and the code sits at the buffer's address.

Eight bytes is only a push and a ret: hex six-eight, the target address little-endian, hex c-three ret, and two A's of padding to fill what strncpy copies. Where does the push point? Into the environment: we export a variable holding two thousand A's with our shellcode at the end - a NOP sled - and aim the push anywhere inside it. The processor sleds forward into the shellcode, so the exact stack layout stops mattering and a sweep over candidate addresses finds the shot.

The shellcode is the part that took two sessions to get right. It opens the password file, reads it, and writes it to both standard output and standard error - reading inside the shellcode, before any exec, because a spawned shell drops the elevated identity. Two constraints shaped the code. First, the path /etc/maze_pass/maze3 must be built on the stack with pushes, and every dword must be NUL-free because it all rides through C strings: the fix is repeated slashes - four before etc, two before maze_pass, two before maze3 - Linux collapses them, and each four-byte chunk becomes printable. The chunks are pushed in reverse order, null first, since the stack grows down. Second, the stack reservation itself: sub esp with an immediate-zero-eighty encodes as a four-byte instruction with three NUL bytes in it, which silently corrupted the environment plant last attempt - the shell stripped them at the dollar-cat. The imm8 form, sub esp comma zero-x-seven-f, encodes NUL-free, and the read count of two thousand easily covers the twelve-byte password.

Nasm assembles it to seventy-eight bytes of NUL-free thirty-two-bit code - the size also confirms the imm8 encoding took effect. Then the driver, typed in vi: the sweep builds the push-ret argument for every four-aligned address in a window, skipping any whose packed bytes contain a null, runs the level with the sled exported, and stops at the first run that prints anything. Stage one sweeps the window that hit in the earlier session; if the layout has shifted, stage two widens to a full sixty-four-kilobyte band of the stack.

The run confirms the lesson live: cat shows the script byte-exact, and the sweep's stage one misses - the stack layout did shift, exactly the uncertainty the sled absorbs - then stage two hits at zero-x-f-f-f-f-d-zero-one-zero and the password prints, twice, once per descriptor: that double print is the read-inside-the-shellcode signature. Verification, per the rules: exit, log in fresh as maze three with the password we just read - u i d fifteen thousand three - and cat /etc/maze_pass/maze3 shows the same string. Maze two done.
